subject: Medicine
topic: Acetaminophen Overdose Rumack-Matthew Nomogram and NAC
stem: A 22-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department by her roommates approximately 5 hours after ingesting an entire bottle of extra-strength acetaminophen (estimated dose 25 grams) in a suicide attempt following a relationship breakup. She currently reports mild nausea and epigastric discomfort, but denies vomiting, abdominal pain, or confusion. Physical examination reveals an alert, oriented woman with normal vital signs. Abdominal examination is soft and completely non-tender, with no hepatomegaly, jaundice, or peritoneal signs. Baseline laboratory evaluation demonstrates: AST 28 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, and prothrombin time (INR) 1.0 (all completely normal). Serum acetaminophen concentration drawn exactly 5 hours post-ingestion is 185 microg/mL. Based on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram, the treatment line threshold at 5 hours post-ingestion is 120 microg/mL. Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Initiate intravenous N-acetylcysteine (NAC) immediately according to the weight-based protocol to replenish hepatic glutathione stores and detoxify NAPQI
options.explanation: ACETAMINOPHEN (APAP, paracetamol) OVERDOSE is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States. Pathophysiology: at therapeutic doses, 90% of acetaminophen undergoes hepatic glucuronidation and sulfation, while ~5-10% is metabolized by CYP2E1 into the toxic, highly reactive electrophilic metabolite N-ACETYL-P-BENZOQUINONE IMINE (NAPQI). Endogenous HEPATIC GLUTATHIONE conjugates and detoxifies NAPQI into non-toxic mercapturic acid conjugates. In massive overdose, glucuronidation and sulfation pathways become saturated, shunting excess drug through CYP2E1. Once glutathione stores are depleted by >70%, UNCONJUGATED NAPQI BINDS COVALENTLY TO HEPATOCELLULAR MACROMOLECULES AND MITOCHONDRIAL PROTEINS, triggering oxidative stress, mitochondrial permeability transition, and centrilobular (Zone 3) hepatic necrosis. Clinical stages: Stage 1 (0-24 hrs): asymptomatic or mild nausea/vomiting; Stage 2 (24-72 hrs): right upper quadrant tenderness, transaminitis begins; Stage 3 (72-96 hrs): fulminant hepatic failure (AST/ALT > 10,000 U/L, jaundice, encephalopathy, coagulopathy); Stage 4 (4-14 days): recovery or death. Management: (1) RUMACK-MATTHEW NOMOGRAM: plots serum acetaminophen level against time from 4 to 24 hours post-single acute ingestion. Here, 185 microg/mL at 5 hours is WELL ABOVE THE TREATMENT LINE (120 microg/mL); and (2) N-ACETYCYSTEINE (NAC): the specific, life-saving antidote that serves as a glutathione precursor and directly conjugates NAPQI. When initiated WITHIN 8 HOURS OF INGESTION, NAC provides virtually 100% hepatoprotection. Standard IV 21-hour protocol: 150 mg/kg loading dose over 1 hour, followed by 50 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours.

options.text: Reassure the patient and discharge home with outpatient psychiatry follow-up because liver enzymes and bilirubin are completely normal
options.explanation: Normal liver enzymes at 5 hours are expected (Stage 1); discharging an untreated toxic ingestion of 25 g results in fatal hepatic necrosis and liver failure within 72-96 hours.

options.text: Administer high-dose oral activated charcoal 50 g repeated every 2 hours without administering N-acetylcysteine
options.explanation: Activated charcoal is effective within 1-2 hours of ingestion to reduce absorption; at 5 hours post-ingestion, charcoal alone does not prevent hepatic failure and fails to substitute for NAC.

options.text: Perform emergent therapeutic plasma exchange to mechanically clear protein-bound acetaminophen from the circulation
options.explanation: Acetaminophen is minimally protein-bound (10-20%) and has a large volume of distribution; plasmapheresis is ineffective and unnecessary when NAC is curative.

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.5 mg bolus to prevent delayed hepatic encephalopathy
options.explanation: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist that lowers the seizure threshold; it has zero efficacy for acetaminophen toxicity or toxic NAPQI generation.

topic: Salicylate Toxicity Acid-Base Dynamics and Hemodialysis
stem: A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his family with confusion, rapid deep breathing, continuous ringing in his ears (tinnitus), nausea, and heavy sweating. His family found several empty bottles of adult aspirin in his bedroom. Vital signs on presentation: temperature 38.6 C (101.5 F), blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg, pulse 116/min, and respirations 32/min. Physical examination shows a restless, flushed, diaphoric man who is disoriented to date. Initial arterial blood gas (ABG) on room air reveals: pH 7.46, PaCO2 20 mm Hg, PaO2 98 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 14 mEq/L. Basic metabolic panel demonstrates: serum sodium 140 mEq/L, serum potassium 3.6 mEq/L, serum chloride 102 mEq/L, and serum bicarbonate 13 mEq/L (calculated anion gap = 140 - [102 + 13] = 25 mEq/L). Serum salicylate level drawn on arrival is 92 mg/dL (severe toxicity > 70-80 mg/dL). Intravenous isotonic sodium bicarbonate infusion has been initiated. Which of the following describes the characteristic acid-base disturbance and the definitive indications for emergent hemodialysis in this patient?

options.text: Isolated pure respiratory alkalosis with compensatory renal bicarbonate wasting; hemodialysis is contraindicated due to sudden bicarbonate loss
options.explanation: Salicylate toxicity is never an isolated respiratory alkalosis; uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation generates a severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Mixed primary respiratory alkalosis and primary high anion gap metabolic acidosis; emergent hemodialysis is indicated for serum salicylate level > 90-100 mg/dL, altered mental status, pulmonary edema, or renal failure
options.explanation: ACUTE SALICYLATE (ASPIRIN) TOXICITY produces a pathognomonic DUAL ACID-BASE DISORDER: (1) PRIMARY RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS: salicylates directly stimulate the MEDULLARY RESPIRATORY CENTER, driving severe hyperventilation, marked tachypnea, and low PaCO2 (<30 mm Hg); and (2) PRIMARY HIGH ANION GAP METABOLIC ACIDOSIS: salicylates UNCOUPLE MITOCHONDRIAL OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION, arresting ATP synthesis and stimulating anaerobic glycolysis (lactic acidosis) and lipid catabolism (ketoacidosis), along with the accumulation of organic acids. The net pH reflects competing processes (often near-normal or slightly alkalemic initially, evolving into severe life-threatening academia as toxicity deepens). Management: (1) SODIUM BICARBONATE INFUSION: alkalinizes serum and urine (goal urine pH 7.5-8.0). In an alkaline environment, salicylic acid is converted into its charged, lipid-insoluble ionized salicylate form (C7H5O3-), preventing it from crossing the blood-brain barrier ('ion trapping' in serum) and preventing renal tubular reabsorption, accelerating urinary excretion; (2) POTASSIUM REPLETION: hypokalemia impairs urinary alkalinization because collecting tubules exchange H+ instead of K+; and (3) DEFINITIVE EMERGENT HEMODIALYSIS: indicated for: SERUM SALICYLATE > 90-100 mg/dL (or >80 mg/dL with renal insufficiency), SEVERE ALTERED MENTAL STATUS / COMA / SEIZURES, NON-CARDIOGENIC PULMONARY EDEMA, or REFRACTORY ACIDEMIA.

options.text: Isolated primary metabolic alkalosis caused by vomiting; managed with intravenous hydrochloric acid infusion without hemodialysis
options.explanation: Salicylates cause profound metabolic acidosis, not metabolic alkalosis; infusing hydrochloric acid is lethal, driving unionized salicylate into the brain.

options.text: Perform emergent endotracheal intubation and set the mechanical ventilator to a low respiratory rate of 10 breaths/minute to normalize PaCO2
options.explanation: Normalizing PaCO2 with a low ventilatory rate causes immediate, catastrophic systemic acidemia, forcing unionized salicylate across the blood-brain barrier and causing brain death.

options.text: Administer intravenous deferoxamine chelation therapy until urine turns orange-red
options.explanation: Deferoxamine is the specific chelator for iron toxicity; it has zero binding affinity for salicylic acid and does not enhance salicylate elimination.

topic: Toxic Alcohols Ethylene Glycol vs Methanol Fomepizole
stem: A 48-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive in an abandoned garage next to an open bottle of automotive windshield de-icer and antifreeze. On arrival, he is stuporous, moaning incomprehensibly, and vomiting. Vital signs show: temperature 35.8 C (96.4 F), blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, pulse 108/min, and respirations 28/min. Neurologic examination shows a comatose man who withdraws all four extremities to noxious stimuli, with depressed corneal and gag reflexes. Dilated funduscopic examination reveals completely normal optic discs and retinas without edema or hyperemia. Flank percussion reveals bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates: arterial blood gas shows pH 7.14, PaCO2 22 mm Hg, and PaO2 96 mm Hg. Basic metabolic panel reveals: serum sodium 140 mEq/L, potassium 5.2 mEq/L, chloride 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 44 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 3.8 mg/dL (baseline was 0.9 mg/dL 6 months ago). Calculated serum anion gap is 32 mEq/L. Measured serum osmolality is 342 mOsm/kg, and calculated serum osmolarity is 298 mOsm/L (osmolal gap = 44 mOsm/kg; normal < 10 mOsm/kg). Urinalysis demonstrates envelope-shaped and needle-shaped calcium oxalate crystals with prominent fluorescence under Wood lamp illumination. Which of the following is the most likely ingested toxicant and the immediate first-line antidote?

options.text: Methanol toxicity, causing retinal ganglion cell necrosis and blindness; treated immediately with oral leucovorin calcium monotherapy
options.explanation: Methanol causes optic disc hyperemia and blindness from formic acid; this patient has normal funduscopy and prominent calcium oxalate crystals with acute renal failure.

options.text: Isopropanol toxicity, causing profound ketosis without acidosis; treated immediately with high-dose intravenous sodium bicarbonate
options.explanation: Isopropanol is metabolized by ADH to acetone, producing an elevated osmolal gap and positive serum ketones WITHOUT a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Ethylene glycol toxicity, causing acute tubular necrosis secondary to calcium oxalate crystal deposition; treated immediately with intravenous fomepizole to competitively inhibit alcohol dehydrogenase
options.explanation: This patient presents with severe ETHYLENE GLYCOL POISONING, an automotive antifreeze ingredient. Ethylene glycol itself is relatively non-toxic; toxicity is mediated by its metabolites generated by ALCOHOL DEHYDROGENASE (ADH): Ethylene glycol -> Glycolaldehyde -> GLYCOLIC ACID (the primary driver of the severe HIGH ANION GAP METABOLIC ACIDOSIS) -> Glyoxylic acid -> OXALIC ACID. Oxalic acid binds calcium to form CALCIUM OXALATE MONOHYDRATE AND DIHYDRATE (ENVELOPE-SHAPED) CRYSTALS, which precipitate within renal tubular lumens, producing acute mechanical obstruction, cytotoxicity, and ACUTE TUBULAR NECROSIS with severe acute kidney injury (Cr 3.8 mg/dL). Flank tenderness and Wood lamp urinary fluorescence (from sodium fluorescein dye added to antifreeze) are characteristic. Osmolal gap is markedly elevated (>10 mOsm/kg) early due to the parent alcohol, while anion gap rises as acidic metabolites accumulate. In contrast, METHANOL POISONING (windshield washer fluid) is metabolized to FORMIC ACID, which selectively attacks the retina and optic nerve (OPTIC DISC HYPEREMIA, 'snowstorm vision', blindness) and the basal ganglia (putaminal necrosis), typically sparing the kidneys from crystal deposition. FIRST-LINE ANTIDOTE FOR BOTH TOXIC ALCOHOLS IS INTRAVENOUS FOMEPIZOLE (4-methylpyrazole), a potent, competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase with an affinity >8,000 times higher than ethanol. Early fomepizole halts toxic metabolite generation. EMERGENT HEMODIALYSIS is indicated for severe acidemia (pH < 7.25), renal failure, or high toxic alcohol levels (>50 mg/dL).

options.text: Diethylene glycol toxicity, causing pure central respiratory depression; treated with naloxone boluses and oral activated charcoal
options.explanation: Naloxone is an opioid receptor antagonist that has zero effect on toxic alcohols or glycolic acid-induced metabolic acidosis.

options.text: Paraldehyde toxicity, causing severe corrosive gastritis and pulmonary hemorrhage; treated with intravenous dimercaprol chelation
options.explanation: Paraldehyde poisoning produces a pungent breath odor and non-ketotic acidosis, but does not form calcium oxalate crystals or respond to heavy metal chelators.

topic: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Hyperbaric Oxygen Indications
stem: A 34-year-old pregnant woman at 26 weeks of gestation is brought to the emergency department after being rescued from a burning apartment building where a faulty furnace malfunctioned. Her husband reports that she was found unconscious on the floor for an undetermined duration. On presentation, she has regained consciousness but complains of a throbbing generalized headache, severe nausea, dizziness, and visual blurring. Vital signs show: temperature 37.2 C (99.0 F), blood pressure 110/68 mm Hg, pulse 108/min, and respirations 22/min. Standard non-invasive fingertip pulse oximetry displays an oxygen saturation of 99% on room air. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. Fetal heart rate monitoring demonstrates a baseline of 144/min with moderate variability and no decelerations. Neurologic examination shows disorientation to time and mild gait ataxia without focal motor deficits. An arterial blood gas with CO-oximetry demonstrates: pH 7.34, PaCO2 34 mm Hg, PaO2 102 mm Hg, arterial oxyhemoglobin 68%, and CARBOXYHEMOGLOBIN (COHb) 28% (normal non-smoker < 3%). Normobaric 100% high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather face mask is initiated immediately. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Wean supplemental oxygen to ambient room air because the fingertip pulse oximeter confirms adequate oxygenation (99%)
options.explanation: Standard pulse oximetry cannot differentiate carboxyhemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin, falsely reading 99% despite severe life-threatening tissue hypoxia.

options.text: Perform emergency bedside cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia to rescue the fetus prior to medical management
options.explanation: The fetal heart tracing is currently reassuring; emergency surgery under maternal hypoxemic shock carries extreme maternal and fetal mortality.

options.text: Administer intravenous methylene blue 1 mg/kg bolus to accelerate carboxyhemoglobin reduction
options.explanation: Methylene blue is the specific antidote for methemoglobinemia; it has zero efficacy for carbon monoxide and would further reduce oxygen-carrying capacity.

options.text: Arrange emergency transfer for hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy to accelerate carboxyhemoglobin clearance and prevent delayed neurological sequelae and fetal death
options.explanation: CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) POISONING is a leading cause of accidental and intentional toxic death. Pathophysiology: CO binds hemoglobin with an affinity 200 TO 250 TIMES GREATER THAN OXYGEN, forming CARBOXYHEMOGLOBIN (COHb), which severely reduces arterial oxygen content. Furthermore, CO causes an extreme LEFTWARD SHIFT OF THE OXYGEN-HEMOGLOBIN DISSOCIATION CURVE (Haldane effect), impairing oxygen unloading to tissues. CO also binds intracellular MYOGLOBIN (causing myocardial depression) and MITOCHONDRIAL CYTOCHROME C OXIDASE, arresting oxidative phosphorylation. Crucially, STANDARD PULSE OXIMETRY CANNOT DISTINGUISH OXYHEMOGLOBIN FROM CARBOXYHEMOGLOBIN, displaying a falsely normal saturation (e.g., 99%). Diagnosis requires CO-OXIMETRY. While normobaric 100% O2 reduces the half-life of COHb from ~300 minutes to ~90 minutes, HYPERBARIC OXYGEN (HBO, 2.5-3.0 atm) REDUCES THE HALF-LIFE TO ~20 TO 30 MINUTES, rapidly forces dissolved oxygen into plasma, reverses mitochondrial enzyme inhibition, and significantly prevents DELAYED NEUROLOGICAL SEQUELAE (cognitive deficits, parkinsonism). Indications for EMERGENT HYPERBARIC OXYGEN: (1) CARBOXYHEMOGLOBIN > 25% (or >15% IN PREGNANCY, because fetal hemoglobin [HbF] binds CO with even higher affinity and fetal elimination is prolonged, causing severe fetal hypoxia and stillbirth); (2) LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS / SYNCOPE; (3) SEVERE METABOLIC ACIDOSIS (pH < 7.25); (4) EVIDENCE OF MYOCARDIAL ISCHEMIA (angina, ischemic ECG changes, elevated troponin); or (5) PERSISTENT NEUROLOGICAL OR COGNITIVE DEFICITS despite normobaric oxygen. Because this patient is pregnant, has COHb of 28%, experienced loss of consciousness, and has ataxia, HBO therapy is definitively indicated.

options.text: Discontinue oxygen therapy and initiate oral prophylactic topiramate to prevent delayed post-hypoxic tremors
options.explanation: Withholding oxygen in active carbon monoxide poisoning guarantees progressive tissue infarction and fetal demise.

topic: Cyanide Poisoning Smoke Inhalation Hydroxocobalamin Antidote
stem: A 42-year-old firefighter is brought to the emergency department after being pulled unconscious from an industrial warehouse fire involving burning plastics, synthetic carpets, and polyurethane foam insulation. On arrival, he is stuporous, tachypneic, and vomiting. Vital signs show: temperature 37.0 C (98.6 F), blood pressure 82/48 mm Hg, pulse 124/min, and respirations 28/min. Pulse oximetry displays 98% while breathing 100% oxygen via a tight-fitting non-rebreather face mask. Physical examination reveals soot in his nares and posterior oropharynx, but no stridor, wheezing, or cutaneous thermal burns. The patient's skin appears flushed and pink, and phlebotomy reveals that both peripheral venous blood and arterial blood appear strikingly bright red. An urgent arterial blood gas demonstrates: pH 7.08, PaCO2 26 mm Hg, PaO2 120 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 8 mEq/L. Blood chemistry demonstrates: serum lactate 16.4 mmol/L (markedly elevated; reference < 2.0 mmol/L), and central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) is abnormally elevated at 92% (normal 70-75%). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate targeted pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium nitrite followed by sodium thiosulfate to induce high-grade methemoglobinemia
options.explanation: Nitrites convert hemoglobin to methemoglobin to bind cyanide, but in smoke inhalation victims with suspected carbon monoxide, this fatally destroys oxygen delivery.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous methylene blue 2 mg/kg to reduce ferric iron in cytochrome oxidase
options.explanation: Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia; it does not displace cyanide from cytochrome oxidase and has zero efficacy in cyanide toxicity.

options.text: Infuse 3 ampuls of intravenous sodium bicarbonate as the sole primary pharmacotherapy for lactic acidosis
options.explanation: Bicarbonate transiently buffers acidemia, but fails to displace cyanide from cytochrome c oxidase; cells continue dying from histotoxic anoxia without antidote.

options.text: Administer intravenous pralidoxime (2-PAM) and atropine to reactivate inhibited acetylcholinesterase enzymes
options.explanation: Atropine and pralidoxime treat organophosphate cholinergic toxicity; they have zero binding affinity for cyanide or mitochondrial cytochromes.

options.text: Administer intravenous hydroxocobalamin immediately to chelate cyanide ions and form non-toxic cyanocobalamin
options.explanation: This patient exhibits fulminant CYANIDE POISONING complicating industrial SMOKE INHALATION from combustion of nitrogen-containing synthetic polymers (polyurethane, plastics, wool, silk). Pathophysiology: cyanide (CN-) rapidly binds the trivalent FERRIC IRON (Fe3+) in MITOCHONDRIAL CYTOCHROME C OXIDASE (Complex IV of the electron transport chain), completely blocking cellular aerobic respiration. Cells are unable to utilize oxygen despite normal or high arterial oxygen content (HISTOTOXIC HYPOXIA). Cardinal diagnostic hallmarks: (1) EXTREME LACTIC ACIDOSIS (serum lactate > 8-10 mmol/L in smoke inhalation has >90% sensitivity for significant cyanide toxicity); (2) BRIGHT RED VENOUS BLOOD and ABNORMALLY ELEVATED CENTRAL VENOUS OXYGEN SATURATION (ScvO2 > 85-90%) because tissues cannot extract or consume oxygen from hemoglobin; and (3) Profound hemodynamic collapse (vasodilatory shock, myocardial depression). The FIRST-LINE ANTIDOTE OF CHOICE IS INTRAVENOUS HYDROXOCOBALAMIN (5 g IV infused over 15 minutes). Hydroxocobalamin contains a cobalt center that binds cyanide with higher affinity than cytochrome oxidase, forming non-toxic CYANOCBALAMIN (VITAMIN B12), which is safely excreted in urine. Hydroxocobalamin is PREFERRED OVER TRADITIONAL NITRITE ANTIDOTES (sodium nitrite / amyl nitrite) because NITRITES INDUCE METHEMOGLOBINEMIA; in a fire victim who likely has concurrent carbon monoxide poisoning, inducing methemoglobinemia further destroys remaining oxygen delivery, precipitating fatal anoxia.

topic: Organophosphate Toxicity Atropine and Pralidoxime Sequence
stem: A 52-year-old agricultural worker is brought to the emergency department by coworkers after being found collapsed in a pesticide storage shed. Coworkers state he was spraying an organophosphate insecticide (chlorpyrifos) for several hours without wearing protective respirators or gloves. On presentation, the patient is unresponsive, profusely sweating, vomiting, and incontinent of liquid stool. Vital signs show: temperature 36.2 C (97.2 F), blood pressure 92/54 mm Hg, pulse 44/min (severe bradycardia), and respirations 28/min. Physical examination reveals pinpoint pupils (miosis, 1 mm bilaterally, non-reactive to light), copious foaming saliva and oral secretions, profuse diaphoresis, and continuous generalized muscle fasciculations involving his face, calves, and chest wall. Chest auscultation reveals diffuse, bilateral, loud inspiratory and expiratory gurgling rhonchi and wet crackles ('copious pulmonary bronchorrhea') with severe expiratory wheezing. Pulse oximetry displays an oxygen saturation of 82% on ambient room air. The emergency team establishes decontamination protocols and secures the airway. Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial pharmacologic management sequence?

options.text: Administer intravenous atropine boluses immediately (titrating and doubling doses every 3 to 5 minutes until pulmonary bronchorrhea and bronchospasm clear), followed by intravenous pralidoxime (2-PAM)
options.explanation: ORGANOPHOSPHATE INSECTICIDES (chlorpyrifos, malathion, parathion) and nerve agents (sarin, VX) produce toxic cholinergic crisis by IRREVERSIBLY INHIBITING ACETYLCHOLINESTERASE (AChE) via phosphorylation of its active serine site. This leads to massive accumulation of acetylcholine at: (1) MUSCARINIC RECEPTORS: 'DUMBELS' / 'SLUDGEM' (Defecation, Urination, MIOSIS, BRONCHORRHEA / BRONCHOSPASM / BRADYCARDIA, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation); (2) NICOTINIC RECEPTORS: muscle FASCICULATIONS, weakness, and diaphragmatic paralysis; and (3) CENTRAL RECEPTORS: seizures, coma. THE PRIMARY CAUSE OF DEATH IS ASPHYXIATION FROM COPIOUS PULMONARY BRONCHORRHEA AND BRONCHOSPASM ('drowning in secretions') combined with respiratory muscle fatigue. Management requires a STRICT CLINICAL SEQUENCE: (1) IMMEDIATE HIGH-DOSE INTRAVENOUS ATROPINE: competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors. Start with 2-4 mg IV bolus and DOUBLE THE DOSE EVERY 3-5 MINUTES. Crucially, THE CLINICAL ENDPOINT OF ATROPINIZATION IS CLEARING OF LUNG SECRETIONS (DRYING OF BRONCHORRHEA) AND RESOLUTION OF BRONCHOSPASM (not pupil dilation or heart rate); and (2) PRALIDOXIME (2-PAM): a nucleophilic oxime that cleaves the organophosphate from acetylcholinesterase, reactivating the enzyme. Pralidoxime treats NICOTINIC RECEPTORS (reverses muscle fasciculations and weakness) and MUST BE GIVEN PROMPTLY BEFORE 'AGING' (chemical conformational dealkylation that renders AChE permanently irreversible). However, ATROPINE MUST ALWAYS BE GIVEN FIRST OR CONCURRENTLY, because 2-PAM does not treat acute muscarinic bronchorrhea.

options.explanation: Pralidoxime has no direct muscarinic antagonist activity; withholding atropine allows the patient to drown in lethal pulmonary secretions (bronchorrhea).

topic: Beta-Blocker Toxicity Glucagon and High-Dose Insulin Euglycemia
stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 2 hours after ingesting approximately forty 100-mg tablets of metoprolol tartrate in a suicide attempt. On presentation, the patient is somnolent, pale, and clammy. Vital signs show: blood pressure 72/44 mm Hg, pulse 36/min (marked sinus bradycardia), respirations 14/min, and temperature 36.4 C (97.5 F). Bedside capillary blood glucose is 54 mg/dL (hypoglycemia). Cardiopulmonary examination reveals cold, mottled extremities with weak peripheral pulses and clear lung fields without crackles. Twelve-lead ECG confirms profound sinus bradycardia with a prolonged PR interval (240 ms) and narrow QRS. The patient has received 2 liters of intravenous normal saline and intravenous atropine 1 mg without any increase in heart rate or blood pressure. Which of the following represents the most appropriate next pharmacologic intervention to overcome this receptor blockade and restore cardiac output?

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous propranolol boluses to displace the metoprolol from myocardial receptors
options.explanation: Administering a non-selective beta-blocker during beta-blocker cardiogenic shock further depresses cardiac output, triggering fatal asystole.

options.text: Administer intravenous glucagon bolus followed by a continuous infusion, and prepare for high-dose insulin euglycemia (HIE) therapy if shock persists
options.explanation: BETA-ADRENERGIC RECEPTOR ANTAGONIST (BETA-BLOCKER) OVERDOSE produces life-threatening cardiogenic shock characterized by severe BRADYCARDIA, HYPOTENSION, CONDUCTION DELAYS (PR prolongation, AV block), and characteristically HYPOGLYCEMIA (due to blockade of beta-2 mediated glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, contrasting with CCB overdose which causes hyperglycemia). Atropine and fluid boluses are notoriously ineffective because competitive beta-blockade prevents endogenous catecholamines from stimulating adenylate cyclase. Pharmacologic rescue strategy: (1) INTRAVENOUS GLUCAGON (5-10 mg IV bolus over 1-2 minutes, followed by 2-10 mg/hr infusion): Glucagon binds specific G-protein-coupled GLUCAGON RECEPTORS on myocardial cells that ACTIVATE ADENYLATE CYCLASE INDEPENDENT OF BETA-ADRENERGIC RECEPTORS. This increases intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP), triggering protein kinase A and opening L-type calcium channels, producing potent POSITIVE INOTROPIC AND CHRONOTROPIC EFFECTS; (2) HIGH-DOSE INSULIN EUGLYCEMIA (HIE): if hypotension persists, initiate regular insulin bolus (1 unit/kg IV) followed by continuous infusion (0.5-1.0 units/kg/hr) titrated up, along with concentrated dextrose infusion to maintain euglycemia. In stressed, shocked myocardium, myocytes switch from free fatty acid oxidation to carbohydrate metabolism; high-dose insulin facilitates glucose uptake and improves myocardial contractility; and (3) INTRAVENOUS LIPID EMULSION (ILE) for lipophilic beta-blockers (propranolol).

options.text: Initiate intravenous diltiazem infusion to control reflex sympathetic myocardial workload
options.explanation: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negative inotropes and dromotropes; combining them with beta-blockers produces immediate complete heart block and death.

options.text: Administer oral activated charcoal and perform emergency whole-bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol
options.explanation: In a somnolent, bradycardic patient with cardiogenic shock, whole-bowel irrigation carries an extreme risk of massive pulmonary aspiration and death.

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil bolus repeated every 10 minutes to reverse central cardiodepression
options.explanation: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist that lowers seizure threshold and has zero receptor activity on beta-adrenergic pathways or myocardial contractility.

topic: Calcium Channel Blocker Toxicity Hyperglycemia and High-Dose Insulin
stem: A 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 3 hours after intentionally ingesting thirty tablets of sustained-release diltiazem (estimated dose 7,200 mg) and twenty tablets of amlodipine (estimated dose 200 mg). On arrival, she is lethargic, pale, and dizzy. Vital signs: blood pressure 68/38 mm Hg, heart rate 42/min (sinus bradycardia with first-degree AV block), respirations 16/min, and temperature 36.6 C (97.8 F). Physical examination reveals cool extremities with delayed capillary refill, normal jugular venous pressure, and clear lung fields. Bedside capillary blood glucose demonstrates a MARKED HYPERGLYCEMIA of 384 mg/dL, despite the patient having no personal or family history of diabetes mellitus. Twelve-lead ECG reveals sinus bradycardia, a PR interval of 260 ms, and a normal QRS duration. Intravenous normal saline boluses and intravenous calcium chloride have provided only transient, minimal improvements in blood pressure. Which of the following explains the prominent hyperglycemia, and what is the primary advanced medical therapy of choice for refractory shock?

options.text: Glucagon-secreting alpha cells undergo autonomous hyperstimulation; treated with oral octreotide monotherapy without insulin
options.explanation: Octreotide inhibits insulin release and is used for sulfonylurea overdose; administering octreotide in CCB toxicity worsens hypoinsulinemia and shock.

options.text: Massive systemic release of endogenous cortisol and epinephrine; treated with high-dose oral metyrapone
options.explanation: Metyrapone inhibits cortisol synthesis in Cushing disease; it has zero efficacy for acute cardiovascular collapse from L-type calcium channel antagonism.

options.text: Blockade of L-type calcium channels on pancreatic islet beta cells inhibits voltage-gated calcium influx required for insulin exocytosis; treated with high-dose insulin euglycemia (HIE) therapy combined with intravenous dextrose and calcium
options.explanation: CALCIUM CHANNEL BLOCKER (CCB) TOXICITY (verapamil, diltiazem, amlodipine, nifedipine) is the most lethal cardiovascular drug overdose. CCBs block L-type (Cav1.2) voltage-gated calcium channels in vascular smooth muscle (causing severe vasodilatory shock) and myocardium/SA/AV nodes (causing negative inotropy, bradycardia, and conduction block). A CRITICAL DIAGNOSTIC HALLMARK THAT DISTINGUISHES CCB TOXICITY FROM BETA-BLOCKER TOXICITY IS MARKED HYPERGLYCEMIA. Pathophysiology: glucose-stimulated insulin release from PANCREATIC ISLET BETA CELLS requires extracellular calcium influx through L-type calcium channels to trigger exocytic vesicle fusion. Blockade of these channels produces ACUTE HYPOINSULINEMIA AND PERIPHERAL INSULIN RESISTANCE, resulting in prominent hyperglycemia (>250-400 mg/dL). In addition, stunned and shocked myocardium switches from using free fatty acids to carbohydrates for energy, but is starved of glucose due to insulin deficiency. Standard tiered management: (1) INTRAVENOUS CALCIUM (calcium chloride 10% 1-2 g IV, or calcium gluconate) to overcome competitive channel blockade; (2) HIGH-DOSE INSULIN EUGLYCEMIA (HIE): regular insulin bolus (1 unit/kg IV) followed by continuous infusion (0.5 to 2.0 units/kg/hr) combined with concentrated dextrose (D10W or D50W) and potassium maintenance. HIE acts as a powerful inotrope, restores intracellular myocardial carbohydrate metabolism, and improves microvascular perfusion; and (3) VASOPRESSORS (norepinephrine) and INTRAVENOUS LIPID EMULSION (ILE) for refractory arrest.

options.text: Acute autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells by chemical metabolites; treated with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone
options.explanation: Hyperglycemia is functional due to calcium channel blockade, not autoimmune insulitis; corticosteroids worsen hyperglycemia and do not treat cardiac shock.

options.text: Renal tubular glucosuria threshold elevation; treated with continuous intravenous loop diuretic diuresis
options.explanation: Loop diuretics exacerbate hypovolemia and worsen cardiogenic/vasodilatory shock, precipitating acute tubular necrosis.

topic: Tricyclic Antidepressant Overdose Sodium Bicarbonate Therapy
stem: A 32-year-old woman with major depressive disorder is brought to the emergency department by ambulance after her partner found her unresponsive next to an empty bottle of amitriptyline (prescribed 150 mg daily). Paramedics report she had a generalized tonic-clonic seizure en route that terminated after intravenous lorazepam 2 mg. On arrival, the patient is comatose and intubated for airway protection. Vital signs: blood pressure 82/46 mm Hg, pulse 138/min, respirations 14/min (mechanically ventilated), and temperature 38.4 C (101.1 F). Physical examination reveals warm, dry, flushed skin, bilaterally dilated and sluggish pupils (7 mm), absent bowel sounds, and a palpable distended bladder. Twelve-lead electrocardiogram demonstrates sinus tachycardia, a prolonged PR interval, a WIDENED QRS DURATION OF 148 MS (normal < 100 ms), a prolonged QTc of 520 ms, and a prominent, tall terminal R wave in lead aVR measuring 4.5 mm (with an R/S ratio > 0.7). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacotherapy to prevent fatal ventricular arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse?

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine 2 mg bolus to reverse central and peripheral anticholinergic toxicity
options.explanation: Physostigmine is strictly contraindicated in TCA overdose; it causes complete heart block, intractable ventricular arrhythmias, and fatal asystolic arrest.

options.text: Administer intravenous procainamide 15 mg/kg infusion to terminate ventricular conduction delays
options.explanation: Procainamide is a Class IA sodium channel blocker; combining it with TCA toxicity fatally compounds sodium channel blockade and triggers cardiac arrest.

options.text: Administer intravenous amiodarone 150 mg bolus to treat wide-complex tachycardia and QTc prolongation
options.explanation: Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval and blocks sodium channels; it precipitates torsades de pointes and worsening cardiogenic shock in TCA toxicity.

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate boluses (1 to 2 mEq/kg) repeated to achieve a target serum arterial pH of 7.50 to 7.55 and narrow the QRS complex
options.explanation: TRICYCLIC ANTIDEPRESSANT (TCA: amitriptyline, nortriptyline, imipramine) OVERDOSE is a life-threatening psychiatric and toxicologic emergency. TCAs possess four distinct toxic pharmacologic mechanisms: (1) FAST SODIUM CHANNEL BLOCKADE (Quinidine-like / Class IA antiarrhythmic effect): blocks myocardial fast sodium channels, slowing Phase 0 depolarization, manifested on ECG as QRS PROLONGATION (> 100 ms predicts seizures; > 160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmias/fibrillation), right axis deviation, and a TALL TERMINAL R WAVE IN aVR (>= 3 mm or R/S ratio > 0.7); (2) ANTICHOLINERGIC / ANTIMUSCARINIC BLOCKADE: hyperthermia, mydriasis, flushing, dry skin/mucosa, urinary retention, delirium, and sinus tachycardia; (3) ALPHA-1 ADRENERGIC BLOCKADE: refractory peripheral vasodilatation and hypotension; and (4) GABA-A INHIBITION / ANTIHISTAMINE: sedation, coma, and seizures. The DEFINITIVE FIRST-LINE THERAPY FOR TCA CARDIOTOXICITY IS INTRAVENOUS SODIUM BICARBONATE (NaHCO3). Indications: QRS duration > 100 ms, tall terminal R in aVR, ventricular arrhythmias, or hypotension refractory to fluids. Mechanisms of sodium bicarbonate: (1) LARGE SODIUM LOAD (hypertonic Na+) overcomes competitive blockade of myocardial sodium channels by mass action; and (2) SYSTEMIC ALKALINIZATION (target arterial pH 7.50-7.55): converts the ionized, active drug into its uncharged, neutral form, which has substantially lower affinity for the sodium channel receptor. PHYSOSTIGMINE IS STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED in TCA overdose because it precipitates immediate, refractory asystolic cardiac arrest.

options.text: Infuse intravenous calcium gluconate 2 g bolus as the primary myocardial membrane stabilizer
options.explanation: Calcium gluconate stabilizes cardiac membranes in hyperkalemia, but has zero efficacy in overcoming fast sodium channel blockade from tricyclic antidepressants.

stem: An 82-year-old woman with a history of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 30%) and atrial fibrillation maintained on digoxin 0.25 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and lisinopril 10 mg daily is brought to the emergency department because of increasing weakness, anorexia, nausea, and vomiting for 4 days. Her family notes that she has become confused and complained that lights in the room appear to have yellowish-green glowing halos around them (xanthopsia). Vital signs: blood pressure 92/54 mm Hg, pulse 46/min and irregular, respirations 16/min, and temperature 36.8 C (98.2 F). Physical examination reveals a frail, dehydrated woman. Twelve-lead ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation with a regularized slow ventricular response (complete AV block with junctional escape at 44/min), scooped, down-sloping ST-segment depressions in leads V4-V6 ('reverse tick' sign), and frequent multifocal ventricular premature complexes with brief runs of bidirectional ventricular tachycardia. Laboratory studies demonstrate: blood urea nitrogen 52 mg/dL, serum creatinine 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL), serum potassium 6.2 mEq/L (markedly elevated), and serum digoxin concentration 4.8 ng/mL (therapeutic range 0.5-0.9 ng/mL). Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive therapeutic management?

options.text: Administer intravenous calcium chloride 1 g bolus immediately to stabilize cardiac myocyte membranes against hyperkalemia
options.explanation: Intravenous calcium in digoxin toxicity is historically contraindicated because excessive intracellular calcium causes irreversible tetanic myocardial arrest ('stone heart').

options.text: Perform emergent therapeutic hemodialysis as the primary modality to eliminate circulating digoxin
options.explanation: Digoxin has a massive volume of distribution (5-8 L/kg) and binds extensively to skeletal muscle; hemodialysis clears <3% of total body digoxin and is useless.

subject: Medicine
topic: Sulfonylurea-Induced Hypoglycemia and Octreotide Therapy
stem: An 76-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and stage 3b chronic kidney disease (baseline eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m^2) is brought to the emergency department after her daughter found her unconscious, diaphoric, and confused at home. Her medications include glimepiride 4 mg daily and atorvastatin 20 mg daily. On arrival, bedside point-of-care capillary blood glucose is 28 mg/dL. The emergency physician administers an intravenous bolus of 50 mL of 50% dextrose (D50W), followed by a continuous infusion of 10% dextrose (D10W) at 100 mL/hr. The patient rapidly awakens and becomes fully oriented with blood glucose rising to 142 mg/dL. However, 2 hours later, while the D10W infusion is running, the patient becomes acutely lethargic and confused again; repeat blood glucose drops to 34 mg/dL. Another bolus of D50W is administered, but 90 minutes later she becomes hypoglycemic again (glucose 38 mg/dL). Which of the following is the primary mechanism driving this recurrent hypoglycemia, and what is the definitive pharmacologic antidote?

options.text: Exogenous dextrose boluses trigger glucose-mediated stimulation of sulfonylurea-sensitized beta-cell insulin secretion; treated with subcutaneous or intravenous octreotide to inhibit insulin exocytosis
options.explanation: SULFONYLUREA OVERDOSE OR ACCUMULATION (glimepiride, glyburide, glipizide) is a frequent cause of severe, prolonged, refractory hypoglycemia, especially in elderly patients with CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE (active metabolites of glimepiride and glyburide are renally cleared and accumulate). Mechanism of sulfonylureas: bind SUR1 subunits of ATP-sensitive K+ channels on pancreatic beta cells, closing channels, inducing depolarization, opening calcium channels, and stimulating continuous insulin secretion. A major clinical trap is the RECURRENT HYPOGLYCEMIA PHENOMENON: administering repeated boluses of concentrated INTRAVENOUS DEXTROSE (D50W) sharply spikes blood glucose, which DIRECTLY ENERGIZES AND STIMULATES THE SULFONYLUREA-BOUND BETA CELLS TO RELEASE MASSIVE REBOUND SURGES OF ENDOGENOUS INSULIN. This produces a vicious cycle of recurrent, refractory hypoglycemia. The DEFINITIVE SPECIFIC ANTIDOTE IS OCTREOTIDE (50 to 100 microg subcutaneously or IV every 8 to 12 hours). Octreotide is a synthetic somatostatin analog that binds G-protein-coupled SOMATOSTATIN RECEPTOR SUBTYPE 2 (SSTR2) on pancreatic beta cells, blocking voltage-gated calcium influx and COMPLETELY SUPPRESSING GLUCOSE-STIMULATED INSULIN SECRETION. Octreotide halts the cycle of hyperinsulinemia, stabilizes blood glucose, and prevents rebound hypoglycemia.

options.text: Complete hepatic glycogen depletion; treated with continuous intravenous glucagon infusion as sole therapy
options.explanation: Glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis, but in sulfonylurea toxicity, hepatic glycogen is rapidly exhausted, and glucagon directly stimulates further beta-cell insulin secretion.

options.explanation: The patient is taking glimepiride and has renal failure causing drug accumulation; suspecting an acute insulinoma and performing surgery is a disastrous misdiagnosis.

options.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors promote urinary glucose loss, which would critically exacerbate life-threatening hypoglycemia in a patient with a blood glucose of 34 mg/dL.

options.explanation: Hypoglycemia is driven by sulfonylurea-mediated hyperinsulinemia; mineralocorticoid fludrocortisone does not suppress pancreatic insulin release.

subject: Pediatrics
topic: Acute Iron Poisoning Clinical Stages and Deferoxamine
stem: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother approximately 2 hours after swallowing an unknown quantity of her mother's prenatal dietary supplement tablets (each containing 65 mg of elemental iron as ferrous sulfate). The mother discovered an open, empty bottle that originally contained 60 tablets. One hour after ingestion, the child developed severe vomiting, retching, and two episodes of hematemesis (bright red blood and coffee-ground material) accompanied by explosive bloody diarrhea (melena/hematochezia). On arrival, the child is pale, lethargic, and irritable. Vital signs: blood pressure 76/44 mm Hg, pulse 154/min, and respirations 28/min. Physical examination demonstrates cold extremities, capillary refill of 4 seconds, and diffuse abdominal tenderness with involuntary guarding. An abdominal radiograph reveals multiple dense, radiopaque pills clustered within the stomach and duodenum. An arterial blood gas demonstrates a severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis with pH 7.16 and serum lactate 8.2 mmol/L. Serum iron level drawn 2 hours post-ingestion is 680 microg/dL (severe toxicity > 500 microg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate specific antidote and clinical monitoring endpoint?

options.text: Administer oral activated charcoal 1 g/kg repeated every 4 hours for 3 doses
options.explanation: Iron is a small heavy metal that does NOT adsorb to activated charcoal; charcoal is completely ineffective for iron toxicity and obscures endoscopy.

options.text: Initiate intravenous deferoxamine chelation therapy, monitoring for resolution of metabolic acidosis and clearance of 'vin rosé' (reddish-orange) ferrioxamine in the urine
options.explanation: ACUTE IRON POISONING is a leading cause of pediatric toxic death. Ingestion of >40-60 mg/kg of elemental iron produces severe life-threatening toxicity. Pathophysiology: free circulating iron generates reactive hydroxyl radicals via the Fenton reaction, causing direct mucosal corrosion, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial membrane destruction, uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation, and capillary leak. Classical clinical progression occurs in 5 STAGES: (1) Stage 1 (0-6 hrs): GASTROINTESTINAL TOXICITY (severe vomiting, hematemesis, bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain); (2) Stage 2 (6-24 hrs): LATENT / STABILITY PHASE (GI symptoms subside, falsely suggesting recovery, while cellular mitochondrial toxicity continues); (3) Stage 3 (12-48 hrs): CARDIOPULMONARY AND METABOLIC COLLAPSE (severe lactic acidosis, vasodilatory/hypovolemic shock, ARDS); (4) Stage 4 (2-5 days): FULMINANT HEPATIC NECROSIS (jaundice, coagulopathy); and (5) Stage 5 (2-6 weeks): GASTRIC OUTLET OBSTRUCTION (cicatricial fibrotic strictures of the pylorus or antrum). Radiopaque pills on KUB and serum iron > 500 microg/dL confirm severe toxicity. Management: (1) Aggressive IV crystalloid resuscitation; and (2) SPECIFIC CHELATOR: INTRAVENOUS DEFEROXAMINE (15 mg/kg/hr IV continuous infusion). Deferoxamine binds free ferric iron to form stable, water-soluble FERRIOXAMINE, which is excreted by the kidneys, classically turning urine a distinct 'VIN ROSÉ' (reddish-orange) color. Deferoxamine is continued until the patient is clinically stable, acidosis has resolved, and the urine vin rosé color clears.

options.text: Initiate oral penicillamine chelation therapy targeting enteric iron crystallization
options.explanation: Penicillamine chelates copper and cystine, having zero role in acute heavy metal iron toxicity and failing to stop mitochondrial shock.

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate to achieve urinary alkalinization and promote iron precipitation
options.explanation: Alkaline diuresis does not enhance iron elimination and promotes ferric hydroxide precipitation in tissues, worsening toxicity.

options.text: Perform emergent total gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y reconstruction to remove corrosive mucosal injury
options.explanation: Total gastrectomy is an extreme, disfiguring surgery completely unwarranted for acute iron poisoning; deferoxamine chelation cures toxicity.

subject: Medicine
topic: Adult Lead Toxicity Occupational Plumbism and Succimer
stem: A 44-year-old man presents to the occupational medicine clinic complaining of chronic, severe colicky abdominal pain, persistent constipation, fatigue, cognitive 'brain fog,' and progressive weakness in his hands over the past 4 months. He has worked for the past 6 years at a commercial lead-acid battery manufacturing and recycling facility, where he admits to inconsistent use of personal protective equipment and occasionally eating lunch in the workshop area. Physical examination reveals an alert man with pale conjunctivae. Inspection of the oral cavity reveals a prominent, hyperpigmented bluish-black line along the gingival margins abutting the teeth (Burton line). Neurologic examination demonstrates bilateral upper extremity motor weakness that is strikingly more pronounced in wrist and finger extensors (bilateral wrist drop) with preserved sensory perception. Complete blood count demonstrates: hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 74 fL (microcytic anemia), and normal platelet and white blood cell counts. Peripheral blood smear reveals prominent BASOPHILIC STIPPLING of erythrocytes. Serum creatinine and liver transaminases are normal. Confirmatory whole blood lead level (BLL) is markedly elevated at 78 microg/dL (normal < 5 microg/dL; OSHA medical removal threshold >= 50-60 microg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Prescribe oral iron sulfate 325 mg three times daily and allow the patient to continue working in the battery plant without restrictions
options.explanation: Microcytic anemia here is caused by lead-induced enzyme inhibition, not simple iron deficiency; iron does not treat lead toxicity and continued exposure leads to nephropathy and encephalopathy.

options.text: Administer intramuscular pralidoxime (2-PAM) and high-dose intravenous atropine
options.explanation: Pralidoxime and atropine treat organophosphate poisoning; they do not chelate heavy metals or clear lead from bone and soft tissues.

options.text: Immediately remove the patient from the occupational lead exposure environment, report the case to public health/OSHA authorities, and initiate oral chelation therapy with succimer (DMSA) or parenteral calcium disodium EDTA
options.explanation: This patient exhibits severe CHRONIC ADULT LEAD TOXICITY (PLUMBISM), acquired occupationally (battery manufacturing, smelting, radiator repair, demolition/painting). Pathophysiology: lead binds sulfhydryl groups on multiple enzymes: (1) Inactivates DELTA-AMINOLEVULINIC ACID DEHYDRATASE (ALAD) and FERROCHELATASE, blocking heme synthesis, causing microcytic anemia with elevated zinc protoporphyrin; (2) Inhibits PYRIMIDINE 5'-NUCLEOTIDASE, preventing ribosomal RNA degradation, producing coarse BASOPHILIC STIPPLING on peripheral blood smear; (3) Inactivates sulfhydryl enzymes in vascular smooth muscle and enteric nerves, causing severe, episodic ABDOMINAL COLIC ('lead colic') and constipation; (4) Causes segmental demyelination and axonal degeneration of peripheral motor nerves, classically manifesting as BILATERAL MOTOR PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY WITH WRIST DROP AND FOOT DROP (sparing sensory nerves); and (5) Subepithelial deposition of lead sulfide precipitating with bacterial hydrogen sulfide in the gingival sulcus produces the bluish-purple BURTON LINE. Management: (1) IMMEDIATE OCCUPATIONAL REMOVAL (mandatory OSHA medical removal protection for BLL >= 50-60 microg/dL) and workplace inspection; and (2) CHELATION THERAPY: for symptomatic adult plumbism or BLL >= 70-80 microg/dL, initiate ORAL SUCCIMER (dimercaptosuccinic acid, DMSA) or INTRAVENOUS CALCIUM DISODIUM EDTA (CaNa2-EDTA). Note that BAL (dimercaprol) is co-administered with EDTA for severe lead encephalopathy, but calcium EDTA alone without BAL must never be given alone in encephalopathy.

options.text: Perform bilateral surgical carpal tunnel release to decompress the median nerves at the wrist
options.explanation: The patient has motor extensor weakness (radial nerve distribution: wrist drop) sparing sensory fibers, caused by lead axonopathy, not median nerve carpal tunnel entrapment.

options.text: Initiate oral d-penicillamine monotherapy while continuing full-time battery recycling work
options.explanation: Penicillamine is an inferior second-line chelator with significant nephrotoxic/allergic risks; chelating a patient without removing them from ongoing occupational exposure dramatically increases lead absorption.

subject: Medicine
topic: Methemoglobinemia Methylene Blue and G6PD Deficiency
stem: A 28-year-old man with leprosy receiving daily oral dapsone therapy presents to the emergency department with progressive fatigue, shortness of breath, and blue-gray discoloration of his lips and fingers for 24 hours. Physical examination reveals an alert man with striking slate-blue cyanosis of his lips, tongue, and nail beds that does not improve after 15 minutes of breathing 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather face mask. Vital signs: blood pressure 118/74 mm Hg, pulse 106/min, and respirations 22/min. Standard fingertip pulse oximetry displays an oxygen saturation of 85% and remains fixed at 85% despite supplemental oxygen. Arterial puncture yields blood that is visibly dark, chocolate-brown in color and fails to turn bright red upon exposure to air. An arterial blood gas with co-oximetry demonstrates: pH 7.38, PaCO2 36 mm Hg, PaO2 184 mm Hg, and calculated METHEMOGLOBIN (MetHb) of 34% (normal < 1.5%). His medical chart reveals a documented history of severe erythrocyte glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. Which of the following is the most appropriate management regarding antidote selection for this patient?

options.text: Administer intravenous methylene blue 2 mg/kg bolus immediately as the mandatory first-line antidote for all patients regardless of enzymatic status
options.explanation: Methylene blue requires NADPH generated by G6PD; administering it to a G6PD-deficient patient fails to treat methemoglobinemia and precipitates fatal massive hemolysis.

options.text: Administer intravenous deferoxamine chelation therapy to chelate the ferric iron from the hemoglobin molecule
options.explanation: Deferoxamine chelates free iron in acute iron poisoning; it cannot access iron bound inside the porphyrin ring of hemoglobin.

options.text: Infuse intravenous sodium nitrite followed by sodium thiosulfate to induce further methemoglobin binding
options.explanation: Sodium nitrite is an oxidizing agent that creates methemoglobin (used in cyanide poisoning); giving it to an already methemoglobinemic patient is lethal.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and avoid methylene blue, because methylene blue is ineffective and can trigger massive, life-threatening hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency
options.explanation: METHEMOGLOBINEMIA occurs when the ferrous iron (Fe2+) in hemoglobin heme moieties is oxidized to the FERRIC (Fe3+) STATE. Ferric iron cannot bind oxygen; furthermore, it allosterically shifts the remaining normal heme groups to the left, impairing oxygen delivery to tissues. Triggers: oxidizing drugs such as DAPSONE, TOPICAL ANESTHETICS (BENZOCAINE spray used for transesophageal echocardiography or endoscopy, prilocaine), NITRITES/NITRATES, and sulfonamides. Diagnostic triad: (1) REFRACTORY CYANOSIS unresponsive to 100% oxygen; (2) FINGERTIP PULSE OXIMETRY FIXED AT APPROXIMATELY 85% (methemoglobin absorbs both 660 nm and 940 nm wavelengths equally, confounding standard dual-wavelength oximeters into calculating an R-ratio of 1.0, which corresponds mathematically to 85%); (3) CHOCOLATE-BROWN BLOOD that does not turn red with oxygenation; and (4) High PaO2 on ABG (dissolved oxygen is normal) with elevated MetHb on CO-OXIMETRY. Standard first-line therapy for symptomatic MetHb > 20-30% is INTRAVENOUS METHYLENE BLUE (1-2 mg/kg), which acts as a cofactor for NADPH-methemoglobin reductase to reduce MetHb back to Fe2+ hemoglobin. HOWEVER, A CRITICAL CONTRAINDICATION IS G6PD DEFICIENCY: NADPH-methemoglobin reductase requires NADPH generated exclusively by the G6PD/pentose phosphate pathway. In G6PD deficiency: (1) Methylene blue CANNOT BE REDUCED TO LEUCOMETHYLENE BLUE, rendering it completely INEFFECTIVE; and (2) Unreduced methylene blue acts as an oxidant, directly triggering CATASTROPHIC MASSIVE INTRAVASCULAR HEMOLYSIS AND ACUTE RENAL FAILURE. Therefore, IN G6PD-DEFICIENT PATIENTS, METHYLENE BLUE IS STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED; FIRST-LINE MANAGEMENT IS HIGH-DOSE INTRAVENOUS ASCORBIC ACID (VITAMIN C) or emergent exchange transfusion.

options.text: Discontinue dapsone and observe without pharmacotherapy because methemoglobinemia resolves spontaneously within 2 hours
options.explanation: Dapsone has a prolonged elimination half-life (30 hours) with active hydroxylamine metabolites; withholding therapy at MetHb 34% leads to fatal tissue anoxia.

subject: Medicine
topic: Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity Intravenous Lipid Emulsion
stem: A 56-year-old woman undergoing an elective open reduction and internal fixation of an ankle fracture receives an ultrasound-guided popliteal sciatic nerve block using 20 mL of 0.5% bupivacaine. Approximately 90 seconds after injection, the patient suddenly reports an intense metallic taste in her mouth, numbness and tingling around her lips and tongue, and a loud ringing sound in both ears (tinnitus). Within 30 seconds, she becomes acutely agitated, develops slurred speech, and suffers a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting 45 seconds. The surgical team administers intravenous midazolam 2 mg, which terminates the motor seizure. However, 1 minute later, the patient becomes unresponsive and cyanotic. Bedside telemetry demonstrates rapid, wide-complex polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that rapidly deteriorates into pulseless ventricular fibrillation and cardiovascular collapse. Pulse is absent, and chest compressions are initiated immediately according to ACLS guidelines. Which of the following is the most appropriate specific pharmacologic antidote to administer immediately alongside resuscitation?

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous lidocaine 1.5 mg/kg bolus to suppress ventricular fibrillation
options.explanation: Lidocaine is a Class IB local anesthetic with identical sodium channel blocking action; administering lidocaine in LAST compounds toxic anesthetic burden, cementing fatal asystole.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous flumazenil 1 mg bolus repeated every 2 minutes
options.explanation: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist that lowers the seizure threshold; it has zero binding affinity for local anesthetics or cardiac sodium channels.

options.text: Infuse 3 ampuls of intravenous sodium polystyrene sulfonate resin into the central venous catheter
options.explanation: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is an enteric ion-exchange resin used for hyperkalemia; infusing it intravenously causes catastrophic fatal microvascular pulmonary embolization.

options.text: Administer intravenous procainamide 15 mg/kg infusion over 30 minutes to stabilize the ventricular myocardium
options.explanation: Procainamide is a Class IA sodium channel blocker; combining it with bupivacaine toxicity fatally exacerbates sodium channel blockade and cardiovascular collapse.

options.text: Administer an immediate intravenous bolus of 20% lipid emulsion (1.5 mL/kg) followed by a continuous infusion (0.25 mL/kg/min)
options.explanation: This patient exhibits fulminant LOCAL ANESTHETIC SYSTEMIC TOXICITY (LAST), a life-threatening complication resulting from accidental intravascular injection or rapid systemic absorption of local anesthetics, most notoriously LIPOPHILIC AMIDE ANESTHETICS (BUPIVACAINE, levobupivacaine, ropivacaine). Pathophysiology: bupivacaine has a very high lipid solubility and strong affinity for cardiac voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav1.5), producing fast sodium channel blockade and slowly dissociating from cardiac receptors during diastole ('fast in, slow out' kinetics). This causes severe conduction delays, refractory ventricular arrhythmias, and profound myocardial contractile depression. Clinical progression: (1) EARLY CNS SYMPTOMS: perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, visual disturbances, dizziness, dysarthria; (2) EXCITATORY CNS PHASE: muscle twitching, agitation, generalized tonic-clonic seizures; (3) CNS DEPRESSION: coma, respiratory arrest; and (4) CARDIOVASCULAR COLLAPSE: refractory bradycardia, AV block, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation, and asystole. The DEFINITIVE SPECIFIC ANTIDOTE IS INTRAVENOUS LIPID EMULSION (ILE, 20% Intralipid). Mechanisms: (1) 'LIPID SINK / METABOLIC SPONGE': creates a new intravascular lipid phase that rapidly extracts lipophilic bupivacaine away from target tissues (myocardium and brain); and (2) METABOLIC EFFECT: directly provides fatty acid substrate to stunned myocardium, overcoming bupivacaine-mediated mitochondrial inhibition. Protocol (ASRA guidelines): 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus over 1 minute, followed by continuous infusion of 0.25 mL/kg/min. subject: Medicine
topic: Severe Heat Stroke Whole-Body Ice Water Immersion
stem: A 19-year-old military recruit collapses during a strenuous 10-mile road march while carrying a 40-pound pack on a hot, humid summer morning (ambient temperature 36 C [96.8 F], relative humidity 82%). When emergency medical personnel reach him, he is obtunded, combative, and disoriented. On arrival at the base medical tent, the patient is unresponsive to verbal stimuli, withdraws non-purposefully to deep pain, and exhibits continuous generalized muscle twitching. Vital signs show: core rectal temperature 41.2 C (106.2 F), blood pressure 86/48 mm Hg, pulse 148/min, and respirations 32/min. Physical examination reveals warm, flushed, moist skin with profuse diaphoresis, dilated pupils, and clear lung fields. Neurologic examination shows severe encephalopathy, bilateral decerebrate posturing to noxious stimuli, and hyperreflexia. Point-of-care laboratory evaluation demonstrates: blood glucose 94 mg/dL, serum sodium 144 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, serum creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, and venous blood gas pH 7.18 with serum lactate 9.8 mmol/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate life-saving intervention?

options.text: Immediate whole-body cold water or ice water immersion (or aggressive evaporative and convective cooling) targeting a rapid core temperature reduction below 39.0 C, while strictly avoiding antipyretics like acetaminophen or aspirin
options.explanation: This patient exhibits fulminant EXERTIONAL HEAT STROKE (EHS), a hyperthermic environmental emergency characterized by failure of the body's thermoregulatory mechanisms during strenuous physical exertion in hot/humid conditions. Classic definition of heat stroke: (1) CORE BODY TEMPERATURE > 40.0 C (104.0 F), measured via RECTAL or esophageal probe (tympanic, axillary, and oral thermometers are notoriously inaccurate and falsely low); and (2) CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM (CNS) DYSFUNCTION (delirium, coma, seizures, decerebrate posturing, ataxia). Note that diaphoresis MAY BE PRESENT in exertional heat stroke (present in ~50% of recruits/athletes), whereas classic non-exertional heat stroke in the elderly typically features hot, dry, anhidrotic skin. Pathophysiology: extreme core hyperthermia drives systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), direct thermal tissue cytotoxicity, endothelial injury, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, and DIC. TIME TO COOLING IS THE CRITICAL SURVIVAL DETERMINANT: 'COOL FIRST, TRANSPORT SECOND.' The GOLD STANDARD AND MOST EFFECTIVE TREATMENT IS WHOLE-BODY ICE WATER OR COLD WATER IMMERSION (cooling rate 0.2-0.35 C/min), rapidly lowering core temperature to a target of 38.5-39.0 C within 30 minutes (cooling is ceased at 38.5-39.0 C to prevent rebound hypothermia). CRITICAL RULE: ANTIPYRETICS (ACETAMINOPHEN, ASPIRIN, NSAIDs) ARE STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED; the elevated temperature in heat stroke is driven by environmental/metabolic heat overload, NOT an altered hypothalamic set-point. Antipyretics have ZERO efficacy and severely exacerbate hepatic necrosis (acetaminophen) and coagulopathy/GI bleeding (aspirin).

options.text: Administer oral or rectal acetaminophen 1,000 mg combined with intravenous ketorolac to reset the hypothalamic set-point
options.explanation: Antipyretics are completely ineffective in heat stroke because the hypothalamic set-point is normal; acetaminophen worsens acute liver injury and NSAIDs exacerbate acute kidney injury.

options.text: Infuse 3 liters of warm 0.9% normal saline over 30 minutes to prevent peripheral cutaneous vasoconstriction
options.explanation: Infusing warm fluids into a patient with a core temperature of 41.2 C severely accelerates thermal brain damage, multi-organ failure, and death.

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg bolus as specific pharmacotherapy for ryanodine receptor activation
options.explanation: Clinical trials have proven that dantrolene has zero efficacy in environmental exertional heat stroke; physical ice water immersion is mandatory.

options.text: Apply isopropyl alcohol-soaked towels across the chest and extremities to promote rapid cutaneous surface evaporation
options.explanation: Isopropyl alcohol soaks carry a high risk of systemic cutaneous alcohol absorption, neurotoxicity, coma, and severe hypoglycemia, especially in children and young adults.

subject: Medicine
topic: Severe Accidental Hypothermia Active Internal Rewarming and ECMO
stem: A 54-year-old unhoused man with a history of alcohol use disorder is found unresponsive in a snowdrift during a subzero winter blizzard (ambient temperature -15 C [5 F]). Emergency medical services transport him to the emergency department while performing gentle bag-valve-mask ventilation. On arrival, the patient is comatose, rigid, and completely unresponsive. Central pulses are barely palpable, very slow, and thready. Vital signs measured with an indwelling esophageal low-reading temperature probe demonstrate a CORE BODY TEMPERATURE OF 24.2 C (75.5 F, severe accidental hypothermia). Blood pressure is 64/38 mm Hg, heart rate is 24/min, and respirations are 6/min. The skin is cold, pale, and cyanotic with generalized muscular rigidity. Pupils are fixed and dilated bilaterally. Twelve-lead ECG reveals marked sinus bradycardia, a markedly prolonged PR and QT interval, and prominent, positive, dome-shaped deflection waves at the J-point (junction of the QRS complex and ST segment) measuring 4 mm in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-V6 (Osborne J waves). Which of the following represents the most appropriate management regarding resuscitation and rewarming?

options.text: Pronounce the patient dead immediately in the emergency department based on fixed, dilated pupils and a core temperature of 24.2 C
options.explanation: Fixed dilated pupils and profound bradycardia are reversible manifestations of severe hypothermia; declaring death before active rewarming to >=32 C violates medical resuscitation standards.

options.text: Handle the patient with extreme gentleness to avoid triggering ventricular fibrillation, initiate active internal and core rewarming (warmed humidified oxygen, warmed intravenous isotonic crystalloid at 40-42 C, and consider venoarterial ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass), and enforce the clinical principle: 'the patient is not dead until warm and dead'
options.explanation: SEVERE ACCIDENTAL HYPOTHERMIA is defined by a CORE BODY TEMPERATURE < 28.0 C (< 82.4 F). Classification: Mild (32-35 C, shivering, intact consciousness); Moderate (28-32 C, loss of shivering, altered mental status, bradycardia); Severe (<28 C, coma, severe bradycardia, hypotension, loss of reflexes, pulmonary edema); and Profound (<24 C, apparent death). Hallmark ECG finding: OSBORNE J WAVES (hypothermic waves), which are positive deflections at the J-point proportional in amplitude to the degree of hypothermia. Critical management rules: (1) EXTREME GENTLENESS: the hypothermic myocardium is exquisitely irritable; rough movement, sudden position changes, or aggressive endotracheal suctioning can easily trigger REFRACTORY VENTRICULAR FIBRILLATION OR ASYSTOLE; (2) ADVANCED CORE REWARMING: passive and active external rewarming (warm blankets) alone are inadequate and can trigger 'CORE TEMPERATURE AFTERDROP' and 'REWINDING SHOCK' (peripheral vasodilation shunting cold, acidotic blood back to the heart). Treatment of choice for severe hypothermia with circulatory instability or cardiac arrest is EXTRACORPOREAL LIFE SUPPORT (ECLS: VENOARTERIAL ECMO or CARDIOPULMONARY BYPASS), which rewarms blood rapidly (1-2 C every 5 minutes) while providing full circulatory support. Alternative active core methods: heated humidified oxygen (40-45 C), warmed IV fluids (40-42 C), and thoracic/peritoneal cavity lavage; and (3) RESUSCITATION MANDATE: hypothermia is neuroprotective against prolonged cerebral anoxia. Fixed, dilated pupils and unrecordable pulses do NOT indicate brain death. The universal resuscitation dictum is: 'A PATIENT IS NOT DEAD UNTIL THEY ARE WARM AND DEAD' (core temperature must be restored to >= 32-35 C before pronouncing death or abandoning CPR).

options.text: Administer rapid intravenous boluses of epinephrine 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg every 3 minutes
options.explanation: ACLS drugs (epinephrine, antiarrhythmics) are ineffective in severe hypothermia (<30 C), accumulate to toxic levels in the cold liver, and trigger fatal ventricular fibrillation upon rewarming.

options.text: Apply rapid active external warming blankets exclusively to the arms and legs while leaving the core unheated
options.explanation: Warming the extremities first triggers peripheral vasodilation, causing cold acidotic pooled blood to rush into the central circulation ('core afterdrop'), inducing fatal cardiac arrest.

options.text: Perform immediate bedside transvenous cardiac pacing to elevate the heart rate to 80/min
options.explanation: Inserting pacing wires into an exquisitely irritable hypothermic right ventricle triggers immediate, refractory ventricular fibrillation.

subject: Medicine
topic: Lightning Strike Reverse Triage and Lichtenberg Figures
stem: During a sudden severe thunderstorm at an outdoor golf tournament, a bolt of lightning strikes a tall oak tree near a shelter where four spectators are standing. Emergency medical personnel arrive on the scene 3 minutes later. A mass-casualty triage protocol is initiated. The four victims are assessed simultaneously: Victim A is screaming and clutching his right wrist with a superficial forearm laceration; Victim B is awake, weeping, and complaining of severe bilateral hearing loss and ringing in his ears, with otoscopy showing bilateral ruptured tympanic membranes; Victim C is conscious, sitting against a bench with extensive, branching, fern-like, erythematous dendritic cutaneous marks across his shoulders and chest (Lichtenberg figures); Victim D is lying supine on the ground, completely pulseless, apneic, and unresponsive with cyanotic lips. Under standard disaster triage rules (e.g., START triage), pulseless and apneic patients are tagged 'Black' (Expectant / Deceased) to direct resources to salvageable victims. Which of the following is the most appropriate management rule for this lightning mass-casualty scenario?

options.text: Follow standard START triage protocol: tag Victim D 'Black' (Deceased) and direct all medical personnel to dress Victim A's forearm laceration
options.explanation: Applying standard triage in lightning strikes is a classic lethal error; pulseless victims of lightning strikes have high survival rates with prompt CPR and should be prioritized first.

options.text: Perform emergent surgical tangential skin debridement on Victim C to excise the branching Lichtenberg cutaneous marks
options.explanation: Lichtenberg figures are not thermal burns and contain no necrotic tissue; they represent cutaneous electron tracking that resolves spontaneously without treatment.

options.text: Enforce 'reverse triage': prioritize immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation and airway rescue for Victim D (the pulseless, apneic victim) ahead of the conscious victims
options.explanation: LIGHTNING STRIKE INJURIES are unique among mass-casualty incidents, mandating a fundamental reversal of standard triage protocols known as 'REVERSE TRIAGE.' Pathophysiology: a lightning strike delivers a massive direct current (DC) countershock (up to 300 million volts and 30,000 amps over milliseconds). This massive electrical discharge causes SIMULTANEOUS TOTAL DEPOLARIZATION OF THE ENTIRE MYOCARDIUM, producing IMMEDIATE PRIMARY CARDIAC ARREST (ASYSTOLE or fine ventricular fibrillation). However, cardiac myocytes have intrinsic automaticity; the heart often resumes spontaneous sinus rhythm shortly after depolarization. In contrast, the MEDULLARY RESPIRATORY CENTER REMAINS SEVERELY PARALYZED for a prolonged duration. If the patient does not receive immediate artificial ventilation, the spontaneous cardiac rhythm is rapidly overcome by hypoxic cardiac arrest, leading to permanent secondary asystole and death. Furthermore, because young, healthy victims often recover completely if ventilated during the period of medullary respiratory paralysis, PULSELESS AND APNEIC VICTIMS HAVE AN EXCELLENT RESUSCITATION PROGNOSIS IF CPR IS BEGUN IMMEDIATELY. Conscious victims (even with burns, fractures, or ruptured eardrums) have already survived the initial strike and are stable. Unique physical signs: (1) LICHTENBERG FIGURES (arborescent, fern-like, feathering erythematous cutaneous arborizations caused by subcutaneous tracking of electrical current and capillary extravasation, pathognomonic for lightning, non-thermal, resolves in 24-48 hours); (2) TYMPANIC MEMBRANE PERFORATION (in >50-80% due to explosive barotrauma from heated air expansion); and (3) Cataracts (delayed complication).

options.text: Administer high-dose intravenous succinylcholine to Victim B to relax laryngeal muscles and prevent post-blast laryngospasm
options.explanation: Succinylcholine induces muscle fasciculations and hyperkalemia; Victim B has isolated acoustic barotrauma (ruptured eardrums) and requires no neuromuscular paralysis.

options.text: Perform immediate bilateral needle thoracostomies on all four patients prior to physical examination
options.explanation: Needle thoracostomy is indicated strictly for tension pneumothorax with hemodynamic collapse; blind needle placement in all victims risks lung laceration and hemothorax.

subject: Medicine
topic: Crotaline Snake Envenomation Antivenom CroFab Indications
stem: A 38-year-old male construction worker is brought to the emergency department in Arizona 90 minutes after being bitten on his right hand by a western diamondback rattlesnake (Crotalus atrox) while clearing brush. On arrival, he reports severe, excruciating, burning pain radiating up his right forearm. Physical examination reveals two distinct puncture wounds 1.5 cm apart over the dorsal first web space of his right hand. There is marked erythema, edema, and ecchymosis extending from the hand to the mid-forearm, with an early hemorrhagic bleb forming at the puncture site. Radial pulse is palpable and capillary refill is 2 seconds. The leading edge of the erythema and edema is advancing visibly proximally by 2 cm every 30 minutes. The patient's friends placed a tight rubber tourniquet around his upper arm and made razor cuts across the puncture wounds in an attempt to suck out the venom. Vital signs: blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg, pulse 112/min, and respirations 20/min. Laboratory studies demonstrate: platelet count 44,000/microL (normal 150,000-450,000), fibrinogen 68 mg/dL (markedly decreased; normal 200-400), prothrombin time (PT) 24.2 seconds (INR 2.2), and aPTT 54 seconds. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Tighten the upper arm rubber tourniquet to completely occlude the brachial artery until surgical exploration
options.explanation: Arterial tourniquets cause complete limb ischemia, massive local tissue necrosis, compartment syndrome, and gangrene; tourniquets must be removed.

options.text: Perform emergency bedside decompressive fasciotomy of all volar and dorsal forearm compartments immediately
options.explanation: Severe swelling and ecchymosis in crotaline envenomation mimic compartment syndrome, but intracompartmental pressures are usually normal; fasciotomy in a coagulopathic patient causes lethal hemorrhage.

options.text: Transfuse four units of fresh frozen plasma and two units of platelets prior to considering antivenom
options.explanation: Infusing clotting factors and platelets without antivenom simply fuels ongoing venom-mediated enzymatic consumption; antivenom must be given first to neutralize the circulating venom.

options.text: Remove the tourniquet, elevate the extremity, measure and mark the leading edge of edema every 15 to 30 minutes, and administer intravenous Crotalidae polyvalent immune Fab (CroFab) antivenom immediately
options.explanation: This patient exhibits severe CROTALINE SNAKE ENVENOMATION (North American pit vipers: rattlesnakes, copperheads, cottonmouths/water moccasins). Crotaline venom is a complex mixture of proteolytic enzymes, metalloproteinases, and phospholipases that cause: (1) LOCAL TISSUE DESTRUCTION: rapid progressive edema, severe pain, ecchymosis, and hemorrhagic bullae; (2) SYSTEMIC COAGULOPATHY: venom enzymes (e.g., crotalase) consume fibrinogen (defibrinogenation syndrome) and destroy platelets, producing marked thrombocytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, and prolonged PT/aPTT; and (3) SYSTEMIC VASCULAR LEAK: vasodilatory shock and neurotoxicity.
